title: The services page a developer-tool company actually needs
metaTitle: Services a developer-tool company should list
excerpt: Describe paid help as an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. The next step is to try the product. A grid of vague capabilities does not help an engineer.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band. The article is about services you can point at on a real screen.
caption: A service offer should be something two people can point at. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a developer-tool services page?
faqs.answer: Each offer needs an outcome stated as a state of the system, a boundary of what you will not touch, and a next step. The next step is to try the product when that is safe. A call can be a second door for the fenced work, not the only door.

faqs.question: Should services come before a trial?
faqs.answer: Send people to the trial first when the tool can be tried safely. The trial shows both sides whether paid help is needed. A page that implies the product does nothing until a statement of work arrives will lose this reader at the install command.

faqs.question: How many service offers should you publish?
faqs.answer: Publish the ones you can staff. A short review and a heavier migration are enough for many tools. A thin block added to match a competitor is worse than a missing block.

markdown:
A developer-tool company services page should describe paid help in the language of an engineer who is skeptical of marketing. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. The next step is to try the product. A grid of capabilities, strategy, and partnership does not help someone decide whether they need you in the repo.

If the tool can be tried without you, say that first. Services are for the gap the trial cannot cross. A page that implies the tool is unfinished until a statement of work arrives will send this buyer back to the install command, and they will not return for the upsell. Be the optional expert, in writing, or be specific about the one job you truly must do for them.

## Name the job in their words

Use headings a maintainer would say out loud. "We wire the tool into your CI." "We migrate the old config." "We sit a review on your first private registry." Skip "solutions" as a heading. It names a department. The job names the pull request.

Say who the offer is for. A platform team adopting it across many repos. A single maintainer who wants a day of review and then to be left alone. Those are different services. Write them as different blocks. A blended offer attracts blended expectations, and blended expectations are how small teams end up in long projects.

Google's people-first guidance asks for content that answers a real task from experience you have. The task here is "do I need your humans, and for what?" Answer it with the work you have done, not with a vocabulary list. If you have only done the work twice, you can still describe it. Do not describe work you have not done in order to look complete.

Keep one offer per block. Onboarding, a migration, and a retained office hour are three offers. Merging them into "success" forces every reader to book a call to learn what success means. The page can tell them.

## The outcome is a working state

Write the outcome as a state of the system, not as a feeling. The pipeline fails the build when the rule fails. The old config is retired. Two people on their side can change a rule without you. A feeling of confidence is not an outcome an engineer can merge.

Name the artifact. A pull request. A documented rule set. A runbook of one page. If there is no artifact, the service is a meeting, and you should call it a meeting with a length attached. Meetings can be worth paying for. They should not be disguised as transformation.

Add the condition. "Once we have read access to a sample repo." "Once a maintainer is named." Conditions keep the outcome from becoming a promise you cannot start. Hidden conditions show up later as delay, and delay confirms the skepticism they arrived with.

Stay inside what you have shipped for others. If the outcome depends on a feature that is still a branch, do not sell the service yet. Invite them to try the current build instead. A service page that sells the roadmap is a marketing page, and this reader came prepared to resent it.

## The boundary is the believable part

Put the fence in the same block. How many repositories. Which CI systems. What you will not rewrite. Their application code. Their cloud account layout. The political decision about which teams must adopt the tool. You can be respectful and still list the no.

A clear fence sounds like this. "We open a pull request for one repository and pair on the first red build. We do not fan the config out to the org." The reader can feel the size. They can also notice if they need the larger offer, or if they can do it themselves after the trial.

The boundary protects the try path. Say what the product already does with no services. Install, sandbox, sample. Then say what the paid block adds. If you cannot draw that line, you are selling a project and calling it a product. Some companies do sell projects. This page should not blur the two, because the homepage told them they could try the tool.

Custom work can exist as its own block with a narrower door. "A scoped change, quoted after we have seen the repo, and only if it belongs in the product or in your config." That sentence keeps one-off heroics from becoming the default. Engineers respect a team that will refuse a fork.

## The next step is to try the product

End each block by sending them to try the product first, when that is possible. The trial teaches both sides whether the service is needed. Say what to look at during the try. Run it on one repo. See the rule fire. Then book time if you want the migration help.

The button or link should use the same try label as the rest of the site. Under it, a secondary line can book a call for the paid block. The order matters. Try, then talk. Reversing the order tells them the trial is a formality and the real product is the invoice.

Tell them what to bring if they do book. A repo they are allowed to share, or a reduced sample. The CI they use. The name of the person who can merge. Three items. A questionnaire of twenty fields will lose the reader you just persuaded to be specific.

If a service cannot be understood without a conversation, still let them try the underlying tool, and describe the call as a review of that trial. "Bring the red build." That is a better meeting than a cold introduction. It also filters people who have not installed anything and want a strategy session you do not sell.

## When a human is actually required

Some tools have a step a stranger should not do alone. A production migration. A security review. An air-gapped install. Say so plainly, and still show a real screen of the tool so the call is about their constraint, not about whether the product exists.

For that offer, the next step can be a short call, with the try path beside it for everything that is safe to touch. Do not hide the entire product behind the one dangerous step. Explain which step is dangerous. The rest should remain tryable. Skepticism grows when a company withholds the safe demo along with the risky one.

Price the required human work as a shape, even roughly. A fixed review. A range for a migration of a named size. "Contact us" with no shape sends them hunting. They will ask anyway. Answer on the page.

Keep this block shorter than you want. The detail belongs in a checklist you send after they are in, or in the docs. The page only has to make the fence and the first step obvious.

## How many blocks to publish

Publish two if that is all you can deliver well. A short review after they have tried it. A heavier migration with a fence. Add a third only for a job that is truly different, such as an on-prem install with its own risks.

Do not add a block to mirror a competitor's menu. This buyer will ask for the thing and then test your depth on the call. A thin block is worse than a missing one. Absence looks like focus. Thinness looks like a brochure.

If a competitor lists a workshop you do not run, let them list it. Your page gets stronger by describing the pull request you actually open. Engineers compare fences, not menus. A shorter menu with a real artifact will win the afternoon they spend evaluating you, which is the only afternoon that matters.

Order the blocks by the path you want a careful engineer to take. Try the product, use the small review if stuck, use the migration if the estate is large. Put that sequence in a sentence at the top so the page has a spine before the details.

If an offer is not staffed, take it down. A services page is a promise that a person exists. Empty promises confirm every doubt the headline already created.

## A block that can go live

Fill this shape with work you have really done.

1. The job, as a heading they would say.
2. Who it is for, and who should just use the trial.
3. The outcome as a state of the system, plus the artifact.
4. The boundary, including what you will not touch.
5. What they can already do with no services.
6. Try the product, and the smaller door to a call if the fence says they need one.

Read the block to an engineer outside the company. Ask what they would do first. If they say "install it," you have the order right. If they say "I have no idea what I am buying," the outcome or the fence is still missing.

Services name the human work. They do not, by themselves, prove who those humans are. The about page has to do that without sliding into a founding myth. Read [how a developer-tool company should write the about page](/blog/how-a-developer-tool-company-should-write-an-about-page) once the offers are specific enough to attach to real people.

When you want those blocks held to a tighter standard, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current page. The useful cut is any sentence that does not change the try path or the fence.
